## What a user of the old system will notice

**Nothing, on the happy path.** Every FIXED behavior — ticket CRUD, the close-idempotency rule,
the "nonexistent ticket returns 200 `{}`, not 404" quirk, the reset flow's rate limit and
non-disclosure-on-failure guarantee — is preserved exactly. A ticket-tracker user clicking
through the UI should see no difference at all.

**Only under failure conditions will anything change, and only for the better.** Today, if the
SMTP server is slow or down, closing a ticket or requesting a password reset can hang for up to
30 seconds or fail outright (PB-001) — after the rewrite (WO-004, pending OQ-002 ruling), those
actions succeed immediately regardless of email delivery. And today, a sufficiently determined
attacker with a narrow guess at request timing has a tractable path to forging a reset token
(PB-002, MD5-based) — after the rewrite (WO-003), that path closes; nothing about how a
legitimate user requests or redeems a reset token changes.

## What's still undecided

Three behaviors that exist in the legacy code today have NOT been ported, fixed, or dropped —
they're waiting on a human ruling (see `decisions.md`'s "Still open" list): whether the
undocumented `X-Internal-Bypass` header on password-reset survives in any form (OQ-001), whether
two newly-discovered crash paths (an out-of-domain `priority` value, a non-string `title` — both
found by the P9 adversarial audit, neither in the original problem brief) get fixed or carried
forward as-is (OQ-005, OQ-006), and whether the CSV export route is dead code to drop or a real
integration to preserve (OQ-003).
